profile.name: Twist
profile.tagline: The 1960s global dance craze where dancers never touch, twisting like putting out a cigarette.
profile.insight: Teenagers invented it in the late fifties, adults made it passé by joining in, and a cigarette-stunting foot movement conquered the world's ballrooms.
profile.profile: The twist is a solo or crowd dance inspired by rock and roll music that became a worldwide craze from 1959 through the early sixties. Popularized nationally by Chubby Checker on American television, the dance requires no physical contact between partners. Dancers rotate their hips, torso, and legs as a single unit while grinding the balls of their feet against the floor as if extinguishing a cigarette.
profile.profile_long:
The twist emerged as a monumental cultural phenomenon in the late 1950s and early 1960s, rooted in rock and roll music and drawing deep historical antecedents from African-American traditions. Having observed teenagers in Tampa, Florida, performing the movement, songwriter Hank Ballard composed 'The Twist' as a B-side in 1959. Recognizing the dance's immense youth appeal, television powerhouse Dick Clark urged Cameo Records to have the wholesome young artist Chubby Checker record a cover. Checker's rendition debuted on national television in August 1960 on The Dick Clark Show, sparking a massive craze that swept the United States and international markets alike.

The mechanics of the dance broke traditional social conventions of partnering by requiring zero physical contact between dancers. Performers stood with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, and arms held out from the body at the elbow. Operating as a single unit, the hips, torso, and legs rotated continuously on the balls of the feet, creating a grinding motion likened to putting out a cigarette or rubbing oneself with a towel. Because the dance required minimal space and zero complex footwork instruction, it leveled social hierarchies on the dance floor, welcoming novices and poor dancers alongside seasoned enthusiasts.

As the craze peaked between 1961 and 1962, high-profile venues like New York City's Peppermint Lounge became temples of the twist, featuring house bands such as Joey Dee and the Starliters. Chart dominance was established through landmark recordings by Chubby Checker, Sam Cooke, the Isley Brothers, and Gary U.S. Bonds. The dance crossed international borders with fierce momentum, particularly in Latin America through Bill Haley & His Comets, and in France where yé-yé stars like Johnny Hallyday launched localized adaptations. Despite drawing parental criticism for its suggestive pelvic rotations, the twist firmly established rock and roll as an accessible, mass-market social phenomenon.

sections.origins_and_history: The twist traces its stylistic lineage to African-American and African traditions, with historians Marshall and Jean Stearns noting that a pelvic dance motion called the twist came to America from the Congo during slavery. Early iterations appeared in blackface minstrelsy with Joel Walker Sweeney's 'Vine Twist' and the early 20th-century craze 'Mess Around'. Blues artists referenced the concept decades prior to the 1950s boom, including Bo Carter's 'Twist It Babe' in 1931 and Jelly Roll Morton's 'Winin' Boy Blues'. The modern dance took definitive shape among teenagers in the late 1950s, catalyzed by Hank Ballard's original song and catapulted to global fame by Chubby Checker's 1960 television debut.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The twist is performed standing with feet approximately shoulder-width apart. The hips, torso, and legs rotate on the balls of the feet as a single unit, with feet grinding back and forth on the floor as if putting out a cigarette. Knees are bent slightly, and arms are held out from the body, bent at the elbow. Hips swivel from side to side while upper body sways, with dancers maintaining a low posture and very little vertical motion, requiring no physical contact between partners.
sections.music_and_instruments: Driven by upbeat rock and roll instrumentation featuring electric guitars, drums, piano, and saxophone, alongside energetic vocal performances. Hit recordings featured driving backbeats and call-and-response structures designed to propel continuous physical movement.
sections.costume_and_setting: Danced in informal youth settings, discotheques, and television stages. Costumes reflected early 1960s casual wear, ranging from teenage skirts and trousers to sophisticated club attire at venues like New York's Peppermint Lounge.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Functioned as a spontaneous youth craze that bridged social divides, transforming rock music into a mass-market phenomenon while sparking generational debates over its suggestive pelvic motions.
sections.notable_figures: Chubby Checker, Hank Ballard, Dick Clark, Joey Dee, Bill Haley, Sam Cooke, Bo Diddley.
sections.regional_variants: Exported internationally, yielding localized versions such as Mexico's 'Spanish Twist' and 'Florida Twist' by Bill Haley, French yé-yé adaptations by Johnny Hallyday and Eddy Mitchell, and British pop versions.
sections.lineage: Influenced subsequent 1960s fad dances including the Jerk, the Pony, the Watusi, the Mashed Potato, the Monkey, and the Funky Chicken.

basic_steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent and arms bent at the elbows.
Rotate hips, torso, and legs on the balls of the feet as a single unit.
Grind feet back and forth on the floor as if putting out a cigarette.
Sway upper body forward and backward while swiveling hips from side to side.
teaching.formation: Solo, in rows, or in a crowded group without partner contact
teaching.level_notes: Accessible to all levels due to the absence of complex footwork or partner connection.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Rock and roll beat with a strong backbeat
music_profile.vocal_style: Enthusiastic vernacular pop and R&B vocals
music_profile.musical_form: Verse-chorus rock and roll song structure
music_profile.sound_description: An energetic rock and roll track featuring a driving drum backbeat, prominent electric guitars, and celebratory vocals commanding dancers to twist.

movement_profile.posture: Low posture with knees bent slightly, torso squared or angled.
movement_profile.footwork: Feet remain in contact with the floor on the balls of the feet, grinding back and forth as if putting out a cigarette.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Held out from the body and bent at the elbow, staying relatively stationary or thrusting in coordination with hip movement.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Hips, torso, and legs rotate as a single unit, swiveling from side to side erotically.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: No-contact solo dancing requiring minimal space, performed individually, in rows, or in a crowd.
movement_profile.partnering: None; dancers do not touch each other.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Fast and rhythmic, matching upbeat rock and roll tempos.

signature_moves.name: Cigarette Stomp
signature_moves.description: Grinding the balls of the feet back and forth on the floor as if extinguishing a cigarette.

signature_moves.name: Towel Wipe
signature_moves.description: Swiveling hips from side to side as if rubbing oneself with a towel.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Low level with very little vertical motion; occasional single leg lifts for styling.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Partner contact and high vertical jumps.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Dance That Started a Global Craze Without Ever Touching
episode_brief.logline: Discover how a teenage dance craze from Tampa conquered the world in the 1960s through simple foot-grinding and pelvic rotation.
beats: Introduction to the 1960s global twist phenomenon and its rock and roll roots.
The origin story: Hank Ballard writing the song after observing teenagers in Florida.
Dick Clark and Chubby Checker bringing the dance to national television in 1960.
The cultural explosion at New York's Peppermint Lounge.
International spread from Latin America to France.
Breakdown of the core movement: the cigarette-stunting foot grind.
Legacy across cinema, music, and pop culture.
